questions.stem: A 54 year old woman with known rheumatic mitral valve disease has a 3 week history of fever, night sweats and malaise. Her daughter says she has become muddled over the last 2 days. Her GP notes that the apical murmur now sounds louder and harsher than at her last review. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever with a new or changing murmur on an abnormal valve is infective endocarditis until proven otherwise; confusion is a recognised presenting feature.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: louder and harsher than at her last review
steps.x: Pre-existing valve disease is a key risk factor, and **fever plus a changing murmur** is endocarditis until proven otherwise.

elim: Rheumatic fever follows strep throat in children/young adults with arthritis and carditis, not a weeks-long fever in a 54 year old.
Meningitis gives headache, neck stiffness and photophobia; it does not change a murmur.
Miliary TB causes fever and sweats but does not alter a valve murmur.
Lymphoma causes B symptoms and lymphadenopathy, not a changing murmur.

steps.x: **C. Infective endocarditis.** Fever + new or changing murmur = endocarditis until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has had 4 weeks of fever and weight loss. He has a bicuspid aortic valve and a new early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. He reports blurred vision in his right eye. His temperature is 38.1°C and pulse rate 98 bpm. Fundoscopy is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on fundoscopy?
o: Cotton wool spots and hard exudates
questions.e: Roth spots (retinal haemorrhages with pale centres) are a peripheral sign of infective endocarditis, caused by septic emboli.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: 4 weeks of fever and weight loss
steps.x: A predisposed valve, prolonged fever and a new aortic regurgitation murmur point to endocarditis; the eye sign of IE is the **Roth spot**.

elim: Cotton wool spots and exudates are diabetic or hypertensive retinopathy.
Drusen are age-related macular degeneration, not an infective sign.
Papilloedema reflects raised intracranial pressure.
Silver wiring is chronic hypertensive retinopathy.

steps.x: **D. Retinal haemorrhages with pale centres.** The eye sign of endocarditis is the Roth spot: haemorrhage with a pale centre.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with a prosthetic mitral valve has a 3 week history of fever. He has several tender, raised, purple nodules on the pads of his fingers and toes that appeared over the last few days. His temperature is 38.3°C and pulse rate 102 bpm. There is a pansystolic murmur at the apex.
questions.q: Which is the most likely name of these lesions?
questions.e: Osler's nodes are painful nodules on finger and toe pulps, an immunological sign of endocarditis; Janeway lesions are painless macules on palms and soles.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: tender, raised, purple nodules on the pads of his fingers and toes
steps.x: **Painful** nodules on the **pulps** = Osler's nodes (Osler = Ouch).

elim: Gottron's papules are scaly lesions over the knuckles in dermatomyositis.
Heberden's nodes are bony swellings at the DIP joints in osteoarthritis.
Janeway lesions are painless flat macules on the palms and soles.
Splinter haemorrhages are linear streaks under the nails, not nodules.

steps.x: **D. Osler's nodes.** Osler's nodes are painful (immune complex); Janeway lesions are painless (embolic).

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman with type 2 diabetes had an infected leg ulcer 1 week ago. She now has 4 days of rigors and is rapidly becoming more unwell. An echocardiogram 1 year ago showed normal valves. There is a new early diastolic murmur. Her temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 122 bpm and BP 96/58 mmHg. Blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in clusters that are coagulase positive.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Rapid, severe acute endocarditis on a previously normal valve is most commonly Staph. aureus, a coagulase-positive gram-positive coccus in clusters.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: gram-positive cocci in clusters that are coagulase positive
steps.x: **Acute** onset on a **normal valve** with coagulase-positive cocci in clusters = Staph. aureus.

elim: Enterococci are chains, not clusters, and follow GI/GU procedures.
Staph. epidermidis is coagulase negative and affects prosthetic valves or lines.
Strep. bovis is a streptococcus (chains) linked to colorectal cancer.
Strep. viridans causes a subacute illness on an already abnormal valve.

steps.x: **B. Staphylococcus aureus.** Acute IE on a normal valve: Staph. aureus, the commonest organism overall.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man had a mechanical aortic valve replacement 5 weeks ago. He now has 6 days of fever and malaise. His temperature is 38.6°C and pulse rate 106 bpm. The sternal wound has healed. Three sets of blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in clusters that are coagulase negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Prosthetic valve endocarditis within about 2 months of surgery is classically Staph. epidermidis, a coagulase-negative staphylococcus.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: mechanical aortic valve replacement 5 weeks ago
steps.x: Early prosthetic valve IE (within **~60 days**) + coagulase-negative cocci = **Staph. epidermidis**.

elim: Coxiella does not grow in routine cultures and follows farm animal exposure.
Enterococci grow in chains and follow GI/GU procedures.
Staph. aureus is coagulase positive.
Strep. viridans grows in chains and follows dental disease.

steps.x: **D. Staphylococcus epidermidis.** Prosthetic valve within 2 months, coagulase negative: Staph. epidermidis.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man had a transurethral resection of the prostate 4 weeks ago, complicated by a urinary tract infection. He now has 2 weeks of fever and fatigue and a new pansystolic murmur at the apex. His temperature is 38.2°C and pulse rate 96 bpm. Blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in chains.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Endocarditis after a genitourinary procedure is classically Enterococcus; the procedure caused a transient bacteraemia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
A **GU procedure** is the source of the bacteraemia, and the organism from the urinary tract is **Enterococcus**.

elim: HACEK organisms are gram-negative and usually culture negative.
Staph. aureus grows in clusters.
Staph. epidermidis grows in clusters and affects prosthetic valves or lines.
Strep. viridans comes from the mouth after dental disease, not the urinary tract.

steps.x: **A. Enterococcus faecalis.** GI/GU procedure before endocarditis: Enterococcus.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman with a known bicuspid aortic valve has 6 weeks of fever, sweats and weight loss. Echocardiography shows a vegetation on the aortic valve. Three sets of blood cultures show no growth at 5 days. After prolonged incubation, the laboratory reports a fastidious gram-negative bacillus. She has no animal contact.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: HACEK organisms are fastidious gram-negative bacteria and a recognised cause of culture-negative endocarditis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
Culture negative at first, then a **fastidious gram-negative** organism = **HACEK** group.

elim: Coxiella is culture negative too, but needs animal (farm, abattoir) exposure and does not grow in routine culture.
Enterococcus is a gram-positive coccus that grows readily.
Staph. aureus is a gram-positive coccus that grows quickly.
Strep. bovis is a gram-positive coccus linked to colorectal cancer.

steps.x: **C. HACEK organism.** Fastidious gram-negative and culture negative: HACEK.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with known mitral valve prolapse has 2 months of tiredness, low-grade fevers and 5 kg weight loss. He has not seen a dentist for years and has several decayed teeth with gingivitis. His temperature is 37.9°C. He has splinter haemorrhages. Blood cultures grow alpha-haemolytic streptococci.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: A gradual subacute illness on an abnormal valve with poor dentition is the Strep. viridans group (e.g. sanguinis), which is alpha-haemolytic.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
**Subacute** course + **abnormal valve** + **dental disease** + alpha-haemolytic = viridans streptococci such as **Strep. sanguinis**.

elim: Enterococcus follows GI/GU procedures, not dental disease.
Staph. aureus is acute and severe and grows in clusters.
Strep. bovis is linked to colorectal cancer and is non-haemolytic.
Strep. pneumoniae is alpha-haemolytic but causes pneumonia and meningitis, not dental-source endocarditis.

steps.x: **E. Streptococcus sanguinis.** Subacute IE with bad teeth: viridans streptococci (sanguinis, mitis).

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with known mitral valve prolapse is admitted with 3 weeks of fever and malaise. She has never injected drugs and has no prosthetic valves. Three sets of blood cultures grow Streptococcus mitis. Her temperature is 38.0°C and pulse rate 94 bpm.
questions.q: Which valve is most likely to be affected?
questions.e: In patients who do not inject drugs the mitral valve is most commonly affected, especially when already abnormal.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
Non-IVDU = left-sided, most often the **mitral** valve; she also has a pre-existing mitral abnormality.

elim: The aortic valve is the second most common in non-IVDU patients.
Eustachian valve endocarditis is a rarity, not the expected answer.
Pulmonary valve endocarditis is rare.
The tricuspid valve is typical in people who inject drugs.

steps.x: **C. Mitral valve.** Non-IVDU: mitral. IVDU: tricuspid.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man is on day 8 of IV antibiotics for mitral valve endocarditis with a large mobile vegetation. He develops sudden, severe central abdominal pain. His abdomen is soft with mild tenderness that seems out of proportion to the pain. He is in sinus rhythm. His pulse rate is 118 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his pain?
o: Septic embolus to the superior mesenteric artery
questions.e: A large mobile vegetation can shed a septic embolus; pain out of proportion to signs with a raised lactate is acute mesenteric ischaemia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: out of proportion to the pain
steps.x: Pain **out of proportion** with high lactate = mesenteric ischaemia. In sinus rhythm the embolic source is the **vegetation**.

elim: Cholecystitis gives RUQ pain with Murphy's sign and fever building over hours.
Pancreatitis gives epigastric pain radiating to the back with a high amylase/lipase.
A perforation gives a rigid, peritonitic abdomen, not a soft one.
Volvulus causes distension and absolute constipation in an older constipated patient.

steps.x: **D. Septic embolus to the superior mesenteric artery.** IE + pain out of proportion = septic embolus to the SMA (acute mesenteric ischaemia).

questions.stem: A 59 year old man is on day 7 of IV antibiotics for aortic valve endocarditis caused by Staphylococcus aureus. He remains febrile. His PR interval was 180 ms on admission. He now feels light-headed. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 38 bpm and BP 100/60 mmHg. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: Rhythm strip on day 7
visual.caption: P waves and QRS complexes are unrelated: complete heart block.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of this ECG?
questions.e: Infection spreading from the aortic valve into the root and annulus damages the nearby AV node, causing PR prolongation and then complete heart block.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: PR interval was 180 ms on admission
steps.x: Ongoing fever on antibiotics plus new heart block in **aortic** IE = **aortic root (perivalvular) abscess**.

elim: He is not on digoxin, and digoxin toxicity gives a reverse-tick ST pattern.
Hyperkalaemia gives peaked T waves and widened QRS, with no cause here.
There is no chest pain and no ST elevation to suggest infarction.
Vasovagal syncope is transient; it does not cause persistent complete heart block.

steps.x: **A. Aortic root abscess.** New conduction disease in aortic IE = aortic root abscess until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman is on day 5 of treatment for mitral valve endocarditis. She becomes acutely breathless and cannot lie flat. There is a new loud pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla and bibasal crackles. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 126 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows bilateral alveolar oedema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her deterioration?
o: Acute mitral regurgitation from leaflet destruction
questions.e: Ongoing infection can erode through valve tissue and chordae, causing acute severe mitral regurgitation and pulmonary oedema (heart failure).

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: acutely breathless and cannot lie flat
new loud pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla
steps.x: A **new pansystolic murmur to the axilla** with flash pulmonary oedema = valve destruction causing **acute MR** and heart failure.

elim: PE gives hypoxia with a clear chest, not a new murmur and alveolar oedema.
Pneumonia gives focal consolidation, not bilateral oedema with a new murmur.
Stenosis gives a diastolic murmur, not a pansystolic one.
There is no transfusion mentioned.

steps.x: **A. Acute mitral regurgitation from leaflet destruction.** IE + new pansystolic murmur + pulmonary oedema = acute MR from valve destruction.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman is treated for native aortic valve endocarditis. Three sets of blood cultures grow Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis). She has had a 4 month change in bowel habit and mild iron deficiency anaemia. She is improving on IV antibiotics.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate further investigation?
questions.e: Strep. bovis (gallolyticus) endocarditis is associated with colorectal carcinoma, so colonoscopy is indicated.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.
**Strep. bovis** means look for **colorectal cancer**: colonoscopy.

elim: CT head is for neurological embolic complications, which she does not have.
OGD looks at the upper GI tract; the association is with the colon.
Renal ultrasound does not look for the colorectal source.
Abdominal ultrasound cannot see a colonic tumour.

steps.x: **A. Colonoscopy.** Strep. bovis on cultures: colonoscopy.

questions.stem: A 49 year old abattoir worker has 10 weeks of fever, sweats and fatigue. He has a known bicuspid aortic valve and transoesophageal echocardiography shows a small aortic vegetation. Three sets of blood cultures taken before antibiotics are negative after prolonged incubation. His temperature is 38.0°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the organism?
questions.e: Culture-negative endocarditis in someone exposed to farm animals suggests Coxiella burnetii (Q fever), diagnosed by serology because it does not grow in routine culture.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.
Animal exposure + **culture-negative** IE = **Coxiella** (Q fever), confirmed by serology.

elim: More blood cultures will stay negative; Coxiella does not grow in standard culture.
Sputum culture does not identify the cause of endocarditis.
Stool culture is not relevant to Coxiella.
Urine culture finds Enterococcus or gram-negative UTIs, not Coxiella.

steps.x: **A. Coxiella burnetii serology.** Abattoir or farm worker, culture-negative IE: Coxiella serology.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with known aortic stenosis has had 3 months of tiredness, low-grade evening fevers and 6 kg weight loss. He has finger clubbing, splinter haemorrhages and a palpable spleen. His temperature is 37.8°C and pulse rate 88 bpm. He is otherwise well enough to work.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A gradual months-long illness on an already abnormal valve, with clubbing and splenomegaly, is subacute endocarditis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: 3 months of tiredness, low-grade evening fevers
steps.x: **Gradual onset** on an **abnormal valve**, with chronic signs (clubbing, splenomegaly) = **subacute** IE.

elim: Acute IE is rapid and severe on a normal valve, not 3 months of mild symptoms.
Rheumatic fever follows strep throat with arthritis and carditis in young people.
Myxoma can cause fever and emboli but does not cause splinters on a known stenotic valve; it is far rarer.
CML gives massive splenomegaly and a high white count, not splinter haemorrhages.

steps.x: **E. Subacute infective endocarditis.** Weeks to months, abnormal valve, mild illness: subacute IE (classically Strep. viridans).

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman with known mitral valve prolapse has fever and a new murmur. Her temperature is 38.6°C. She has Janeway lesions on her palms and painful nodules on two finger pulps. Two of three blood culture sets grow Staphylococcus aureus. Transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiography show no vegetation.
questions.q: Which best describes her diagnosis using the modified Duke criteria?
o: Unable to classify without a biopsy
questions.e: She has 1 major criterion (typical organism on blood cultures) and 4 minor (predisposing valve, fever over 38°C, vascular phenomena, immunological phenomena): 1 major + 3 minor is definite.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.

clues: painful nodules on two finger pulps
Two of three blood culture sets grow Staphylococcus aureus
steps.x: Major: **positive cultures with a typical organism**. Minor: predisposition, fever **>38°C**, vascular (Janeway), immunological (Osler). 1 major + 3 minor = definite.

elim: A normal echo does not exclude IE when Duke criteria are met.
Possible IE is 1 major + 1 minor or 3 minor; she has more than that.
This is not a Duke category; she already meets definite criteria.
Duke criteria are clinical; a biopsy is not needed.

steps.x: **A. Definite infective endocarditis.** Definite = 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man is admitted with fever and a new murmur. His temperature is 38.4°C. He has a prosthetic aortic valve, splinter haemorrhages and microscopic haematuria. Three sets of blood cultures are pending. The team is applying the modified Duke criteria.
questions.q: Which finding would count as a major criterion?
questions.e: The two major Duke criteria are positive blood cultures with a typical organism and echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement such as a vegetation.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.

clues: Three sets of blood cultures are pending
steps.x: Majors are the two cornerstones: **cultures** and **echo vegetation**. Everything else in the stem is minor.

elim: Fever over 38°C is a minor criterion.
A predisposing condition such as a prosthetic valve is a minor criterion.
CRP is not a Duke criterion at all.
Splinter haemorrhages are a vascular phenomenon, a minor criterion.

steps.x: **B. Oscillating vegetation on echocardiography.** Major Duke criteria: typical organism on cultures; vegetation on echo.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman with a repaired ventricular septal defect has 2 weeks of fever, malaise and a new pansystolic murmur. Her temperature is 38.3°C and pulse rate 100 bpm. She is haemodynamically stable. Her GP has referred her to the medical team, who suspect infective endocarditis.
questions.q: Which combination of investigations forms the basis of the diagnosis?
questions.e: Blood cultures and echocardiography are the gold standard, formalised in the modified Duke criteria.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.

clues: fever, malaise and a new pansystolic murmur
steps.x: Congenital heart disease is a risk factor. The Duke major criteria rest on **cultures** and **echo**.

elim: CXR and ECG look for complications, not the diagnosis.
CRP and ESR are raised but non-specific.
CT can look for emboli but does not diagnose IE.
Urinalysis may show haematuria but is non-specific.

steps.x: **A. Blood cultures and echocardiography.** Gold standard: blood cultures + echocardiography (modified Duke criteria).

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with a native bicuspid aortic valve has 3 weeks of fever and fatigue. There is a new early diastolic murmur. Three sets of blood cultures have been taken from different sites. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 132/62 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial imaging investigation?
questions.e: Transthoracic echocardiography is the first-line non-invasive imaging for suspected native valve endocarditis.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.

clues: Three sets of blood cultures have been taken
steps.x: Cultures are done; the next test is the **first-line, non-invasive** echo: **TTE**.

elim: Cardiac MRI is not a first-line test for vegetations.
CT coronary angiography assesses coronary disease.
PET-CT is a specialist adjunct, mainly for prosthetic valves.
TOE is invasive and second-line, used if TTE is inconclusive or for prosthetic valves.

steps.x: **E. Transthoracic echocardiography.** Native valve, suspected IE: TTE first, TOE if inconclusive.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has 4 weeks of fever, night sweats and a new apical pansystolic murmur. She has splinter haemorrhages and Janeway lesions. Three sets of blood cultures grow Streptococcus mitis. Transthoracic echocardiography is technically difficult and shows no vegetation. Her temperature is 38.4°C.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: TOE is more sensitive than TTE and is used when suspicion remains high despite a normal or poor-quality TTE.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.

clues: Three sets of blood cultures grow Streptococcus mitis
technically difficult and shows no vegetation
steps.x: Suspicion is **high** but TTE was negative: move to the more sensitive **TOE**.

elim: Catheterisation is invasive and risks dislodging vegetations.
CTPA looks for pulmonary emboli.
Waiting 6 months delays a diagnosis that changes treatment now.
Stress echo assesses ischaemia, not vegetations.

steps.x: **E. Transoesophageal echocardiography.** High suspicion, normal TTE: TOE.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with a known mitral regurgitation murmur is brought to A&E with fever and confusion. His temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 78/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. His lactate is 5.8 mmol/L. One set of blood cultures has been taken.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Take two more culture sets 6 hours apart before antibiotics
questions.e: Three culture sets are ideal before antibiotics, but in a septic, shocked patient treatment must not be delayed.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.

clues: One set of blood cultures has been taken
steps.x: He is in **septic shock**. The rule of three culture sets first is broken when the patient is septic.

elim: Echocardiography is needed but must not delay antibiotics in shock.
Endocarditis needs IV, not oral, antibiotics.
Spacing cultures over hours is for stable patients; he is shocked.
Sensitivities take days; he needs empirical treatment now.

steps.x: **B. Give empirical IV antibiotics now.** Septic patient: take what cultures you can, but do not delay IV antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman with congenital aortic stenosis has 5 weeks of fever, malaise and weight loss. Her temperature is 38.0°C. Blood cultures are pending. Her GP sent routine bloods last week.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on her blood tests?
questions.e: Infective endocarditis typically raises both CRP and ESR as part of the inflammatory response.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.

clues: 5 weeks of fever, malaise and weight loss
steps.x: Weeks of infection on an abnormal valve: expect raised inflammatory markers, **both CRP and ESR**.

elim: A low CRP would be unexpected in active bacterial infection.
Normal markers would argue against endocarditis.
Eosinophilia suggests allergy or parasites, not endocarditis.
ESR is raised, not low, in endocarditis.

steps.x: **C. Raised CRP and ESR.** IE bloods: raised CRP and ESR (non-specific, not diagnostic).

questions.stem: A 62 year old man is admitted with aortic valve endocarditis. TOE shows a 9 mm vegetation on the aortic valve with no abscess. His admission ECG shows sinus rhythm with a PR interval of 190 ms. He is started on IV antibiotics and is stable.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to monitor for a perivalvular abscess?
questions.e: A perivalvular or aortic root abscess is monitored with daily ECGs, looking for a lengthening PR interval or progression to heart block.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.
An aortic root abscess shows itself as **conduction disease**; the cheap daily screen is the **ECG**.

elim: A chest X-ray cannot show an abscess in the aortic root.
Troponin is not used to monitor for abscess.
Weekly CT is too infrequent and not the routine monitor.
ESR trends are slow and non-specific.

steps.x: **A. Daily 12-lead ECG.** Aortic IE: daily ECG, watch for a lengthening PR interval.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has suspected native mitral valve endocarditis. She has no drug allergies and no MRSA risk factors. Three sets of blood cultures have been taken and the organism is not yet known. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial antibiotic treatment?
questions.e: Empirical treatment for native valve endocarditis, without allergy or MRSA risk, is IV amoxicillin (sometimes with gentamicin).

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.

clues: no drug allergies and no MRSA risk factors
steps.x: **Empirical**, **native valve**, no allergy: IV amoxicillin (± gentamicin).

elim: Benzylpenicillin is targeted therapy once Strep. viridans is known.
Vancomycin, rifampicin and gentamicin is the empirical regimen for a prosthetic valve.
Endocarditis needs IV antibiotics, not oral.
Doxycycline is used for Coxiella, not empirical native valve IE.

steps.x: **A. IV amoxicillin.** Native valve, empirical: IV amoxicillin ± gentamicin.

questions.stem: A 43 year old man who is a known MRSA carrier has native tricuspid valve endocarditis. Three sets of blood cultures grow meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg. He has no allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment?
questions.e: MRSA endocarditis is treated with IV vancomycin and gentamicin.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
MRSA is resistant to flucloxacillin and penicillins: use **vancomycin + gentamicin**.

elim: Flucloxacillin is for MSSA; MRSA is resistant.
MRSA is resistant to amoxicillin.
Benzylpenicillin is for Strep. viridans.
Oral clarithromycin is inadequate for endocarditis.

steps.x: **D. IV vancomycin and gentamicin.** MRSA IE: IV vancomycin + gentamicin.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man had a cystoscopy 6 weeks ago. He now has native mitral valve endocarditis. Three sets of blood cultures grow Enterococcus faecalis sensitive to amoxicillin. He has no allergies. His temperature is 38.1°C and pulse rate 92 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment?
questions.e: Enterococcal endocarditis is treated with IV amoxicillin and gentamicin (or IV ceftriaxone and gentamicin).

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
Enterococcus after a **GU procedure**, sensitive and no allergy: **amoxicillin + gentamicin**.

elim: Flucloxacillin is for Staph. aureus; enterococci are not covered.
Metronidazole covers anaerobes, not enterococci.
Vancomycin and rifampicin is for Staph. aureus with penicillin allergy.
Nitrofurantoin treats lower UTIs and does not reach the heart.

steps.x: **B. IV amoxicillin and gentamicin.** Enterococcal IE: IV amoxicillin + gentamicin.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has a bioprosthetic aortic valve inserted 4 years ago. She now has endocarditis of the prosthetic valve. Three sets of blood cultures grow meticillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. She has no allergies. Her temperature is 38.7°C and pulse rate 110 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment?
questions.e: Confirmed MSSA prosthetic valve endocarditis is treated with flucloxacillin, rifampicin (penetrates biofilm) and gentamicin (synergy).

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
**Prosthetic valve** + MSSA: flucloxacillin, plus **rifampicin** for the biofilm, plus gentamicin.

elim: Amoxicillin alone is the native valve empirical choice and misses most Staph. aureus.
Benzylpenicillin and gentamicin is for Strep. viridans.
Ceftriaxone and gentamicin is for streptococci or enterococci.
Oral therapy is inadequate for endocarditis.

steps.x: **D. IV flucloxacillin, rifampicin and gentamicin.** Prosthetic valve MSSA: flucloxacillin + rifampicin + gentamicin.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man had a mechanical mitral valve replacement 3 years ago. He presents with 10 days of fever and a new regurgitant murmur. TOE shows a vegetation on the prosthesis. Three sets of blood cultures have been taken and are pending. He has no allergies. His temperature is 38.5°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial antibiotic treatment?
questions.e: Empirical treatment for prosthetic valve endocarditis with the organism not yet confirmed is vancomycin, rifampicin and gentamicin.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
**Prosthetic** valve and **organism unknown**: cover staphylococci including MRSA and the biofilm: vancomycin + rifampicin + gentamicin.

elim: Amoxicillin is the empirical choice for native valves only.
Benzylpenicillin is targeted therapy for Strep. viridans.
Flucloxacillin alone misses MRSA and coagulase-negative staphylococci and lacks biofilm cover.
Oral linezolid is not empirical endocarditis treatment.

steps.x: **D. IV vancomycin, rifampicin and gentamicin.** Prosthetic valve, organism unknown: vancomycin + rifampicin + gentamicin.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has native aortic valve endocarditis. Three sets of blood cultures grow meticillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. She had anaphylaxis to penicillin in the past. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment?
questions.e: Staph. aureus endocarditis in a penicillin-allergic patient is treated with vancomycin plus rifampicin instead of flucloxacillin.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
MSSA would normally get flucloxacillin, but **anaphylaxis to penicillin** rules out all penicillins: **vancomycin + rifampicin**.

elim: Flucloxacillin is a penicillin; she had anaphylaxis.
Amoxicillin is a penicillin.
Benzylpenicillin is a penicillin.
Co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin.

steps.x: **E. IV vancomycin and rifampicin.** Staph. aureus + penicillin allergy: vancomycin + rifampicin.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has native mitral valve endocarditis caused by Streptococcus viridans. He is on IV benzylpenicillin and has been afebrile for 4 days. His CRP is falling. He asks how long he will need intravenous treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate total duration of antibiotic treatment?
questions.e: Endocarditis needs prolonged antibiotic treatment, typically around 4 to 6 weeks, because organisms inside vegetations are hard to reach.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
Even when he improves, vegetations need a **prolonged** course: about **4 to 6 weeks**.

elim: 10 to 14 days is too short for vegetations.
3 days is far too short and risks relapse.
6 months is TB length, not endocarditis.
7 days is a pneumonia or UTI course, not endocarditis.

steps.x: **C. 4 to 6 weeks.** IE antibiotics: about 4 to 6 weeks.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman is on day 12 of appropriate IV antibiotics for mitral valve endocarditis caused by Staphylococcus aureus. She remains febrile and blood cultures are still positive. Yesterday she had a transient left arm weakness and today a painful cold toe. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Persistent infection despite antibiotics and recurrent emboli, especially with Staph. aureus, are indications for surgical valve repair.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
**Persistent infection** + **recurrent emboli** + Staph. aureus = indications for **surgery**.

elim: Adding drugs does not remove an infected embolising vegetation.
Oral antibiotics are inappropriate for active uncontrolled IE.
Anticoagulation does not prevent septic emboli and risks haemorrhage.
She is on appropriate treatment; changing antibiotic does not address the failure.

steps.x: **D. Surgical valve repair or replacement.** Failure of antibiotics or recurrent emboli: surgical valve repair.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has prosthetic aortic valve endocarditis. Transoesophageal echocardiography shows a cavity in the aortic root next to the valve ring. His ECG shows a PR interval that has lengthened from 170 ms to 260 ms over 3 days. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 112/68 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Insert a permanent pacemaker and continue antibiotics
questions.e: An aortic root abscess is an indication for surgery and needs urgent cardiothoracic referral; antibiotics alone do not drain it.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.

clues: lengthened from 170 ms to 260 ms over 3 days
steps.x: A **root abscess** with **lengthening PR** = urgent surgical problem.

elim: Doxycycline is for Coxiella and does not treat an abscess.
Pacing may be needed, but the abscess itself needs surgery.
Waiting 2 weeks risks complete heart block and root destruction.
Oral antibiotics are inadequate for uncontrolled IE.

steps.x: **E. Urgent referral to cardiothoracic surgery.** Aortic root abscess: urgent cardiothoracic surgery.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman had a mechanical aortic valve replacement 2 years ago. She is due to have two teeth extracted next week and asks her GP whether she needs antibiotics to prevent endocarditis. She has no allergies and is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: IV vancomycin at the dental appointment
No prophylaxis; explain the symptoms of endocarditis
questions.e: In the UK antibiotic prophylaxis is not routinely given for dental procedures, even with a prosthetic valve; patients are advised about the symptoms of endocarditis instead.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
UK (NICE) practice: **no routine prophylaxis**, even with a mechanical valve. Educate about the symptoms.

elim: Routine amoxicillin prophylaxis is not UK practice.
Good dental care reduces risk; avoiding treatment is harmful.
Clindamycin prophylaxis is not routine in the UK.
IV vancomycin is not used for dental prophylaxis.

steps.x: **E. No prophylaxis; explain the symptoms of endocarditis.** UK: no routine endocarditis prophylaxis; teach the warning symptoms.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man is completing 4 weeks of IV benzylpenicillin for native mitral valve endocarditis caused by Streptococcus viridans. He is afebrile and his CRP has normalised. He has poor dentition and has not seen a dentist for 6 years.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate step before discharge?
questions.e: Strep. viridans endocarditis comes from the mouth, so dental review is needed to remove the source and prevent recurrence.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
**Viridans** streptococci come from the **mouth**: fix the source with a dental review.

elim: Colonoscopy is for Strep. bovis.
Lifelong antibiotics are not recommended.
There is no indication for surgery after a cured infection.
Aspirin does not prevent endocarditis.

steps.x: **B. Arrange a dental review.** Strep. viridans IE: dental review.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with degenerative mitral regurgitation develops infective endocarditis 3 weeks after a dental scale and polish. Echocardiography shows a mobile mass on the atrial surface of the mitral valve, where the regurgitant jet strikes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the mass?
o: Direct invasion of normal endothelium by circulating fungi
Myxomatous degeneration of the valve leaflet
Platelet-fibrin thrombus on damaged endothelium colonised during bacteraemia
Sterile platelet deposits in advanced malignancy
questions.e: Turbulent flow damages the endocardium, platelets and fibrin deposit there, and the thrombus is seeded during a transient bacteraemia (here dental) to form a vegetation.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding in the stem to the mechanism behind it.
**Turbulent jet** damages endothelium, a **platelet-fibrin thrombus** forms, and **bacteraemia** from the dental procedure seeds it.

elim: Molecular mimicry is rheumatic fever, not a vegetation.
Fungal endocarditis exists but is not the usual mechanism, and normal endothelium resists seeding.
Myxomatous degeneration causes prolapse, not a vegetation.
Sterile marantic vegetations occur in malignancy, but he has bacteraemia after a dental procedure.

steps.x: **D. Platelet-fibrin thrombus on damaged endothelium colonised during bacteraemia.** Vegetation = damaged endothelium + platelet-fibrin thrombus + bacteraemia.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman who injects drugs has left-sided endocarditis of the aortic valve. She has painless, flat, non-tender red macules on her soles and linear red-brown streaks under several fingernails. Her temperature is 38.5°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of these signs?
questions.e: Janeway lesions and splinter haemorrhages are vascular phenomena caused by septic emboli; Osler's nodes and glomerulonephritis are immune complex phenomena.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding in the stem to the mechanism behind it.

clues: painless, flat, non-tender red macules on her soles
linear red-brown streaks under several fingernails
steps.x: **Painless** Janeway lesions and **splinters** = **embolic** (vascular) phenomena.

elim: Immune complexes cause painful Osler's nodes and glomerulonephritis.
Platelet dysfunction causes purpura and bleeding, not these signs.
Raised venous pressure does not cause these lesions.
Vasospasm causes Raynaud's colour changes, not macules or splinters.

steps.x: **D. Septic microemboli.** Janeway, splinters, Roth spots: emboli. Osler's nodes, GN: immune complexes.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with aortic valve endocarditis develops a PR interval that lengthens daily and then second-degree heart block. TOE shows a perivalvular abscess extending from the aortic valve ring into the interventricular septum.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his conduction disease?
o: Infection extending into the annulus near the AV node
Septic emboli to the right coronary artery
questions.e: Infection spreading into the annulus and myocardium forms an abscess near the AV node and His bundle, causing progressive heart block.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding in the stem to the mechanism behind it.

clues: perivalvular abscess extending from the aortic valve ring into the interventricular septum
steps.x: The aortic annulus sits right next to the **AV node and His bundle**; an abscess there damages conduction.

elim: QT prolongation does not lengthen the PR interval.
Fever does not cause progressive heart block.
Vagal tone causes transient changes, not progressive block with an abscess.
Coronary emboli cause infarction with ST change; the abscess explains this directly.

steps.x: **D. Infection extending into the annulus near the AV node.** Aortic root abscess eats into the conduction tissue next to the AV node.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man who injects heroin has 10 days of fever, rigors and cough. There is a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge. His temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Multiple cavitating nodules in both lungs: septic pulmonary emboli.

questions.q: Which valve is most likely to be affected?
questions.e: In people who inject drugs, organisms reach the right heart first through venous return, so the tricuspid valve is most often affected; emboli go to the lungs.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge
steps.x: IVDU + LLSE pansystolic murmur + **lung** (not systemic) emboli = right-sided, **tricuspid** endocarditis.

elim: Aortic IE gives an early diastolic murmur and systemic emboli.
Mitral IE gives an apical murmur and systemic emboli.
He has no prosthetic valve.
Pulmonary valve IE is rare, even in people who inject drugs.

steps.x: **E. Tricuspid valve.** IVDU: tricuspid valve, with septic emboli to the lungs.
